chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
title: Jimmy Lunceford, Sy Oliver and black arrangers behind white bands
summary: Sam calls Lunceford the greatest band; they discuss white bands taking black arrangements and Eldridge, Shavers, Charlie Barnet.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: See the greatest band man, the greatest band was Jimmy Lunceford. It was the swingerest band in the land
Mmmm.
And even that band, I thought that band was more exciting than the great Duke Ellington band, man.
Mmmm.

Because I had a chance to see, as a teenager I had a chance to see and hear the Jimmy Lunceford band, man. I'll tell you something, man. I ain't never heard anything like that in my life. And I ain't never saw a group of men carry themselves...I think I talked....
You talked about that before.
I talked about that before, man. See I could never forget that. You have to always be in there because...
There were so many of those bands again, you know.
There was a lot of them.
Like Chick Webb and you know...
That band I never saw.

And so many of those bands like they're doing. It seemed like all that stuff was so powerful because Tiny Grimes was telling me about - he was talking about the Jimmy Lunceford band in the same, he was mentioning some of the same things like you were talking about. And he mentioned how, you know that they really had this stuff with the curtain open. You see these cats out there and man it was just - knock you out. Those cats would be so sharp and the music would be hitting.
Sharp and hitting them.
And he said there would be some white cats sitting up in the balcony, you know.
That's right.
Transcribing all these arrangements. And these cats would have perfect pitch and stuff. They'd be able to write out the arrangements. And they'd go back and take it to the white bands.
Right.
And they'd say you know they'd be in them big hotels. They'd be playing these arrangements but it would be Jimmy Lunceford's stuff, you know.
That's right and were 'nt for Sy Oliver, where
would you think Tommy Dorsey would be? You see, they never talk about that.

See that's the thing that always and the minute we start talking about that, we as black musicians then we suddenly - it's Crow Jim, you know or something like that. We're bad guys that we've got a chip on our shoulder.
Well, maybe we have. You know maybe we've got a chip...Shit if you look at it man, if it weren't for R y Eldridge, where would Gene Krupa be?
That's right.
Charlie Shavers. Charlie Shavers, another bad dude, you see.
I alread come down to the Vanguard one night and light the fire on Miles.

Right. That man was fantastic, man. See all those people man and those bands. Where do you think that Woody Herman got his idea of having a jazz band man. He got this stuff from Charlie Barnet. All these styles man come from all those bands recalled you know.
Yeah.
All of them man.
So many bands that really even never got a lot of recognition. Because I remember coming up in Indiana, how many bands. I mean there were hundreds of musicians.
